title: Where is the vibration or noise coming from?
summary: Use frequency, throttle, eRPM, and time behaviour to separate motor-linked ridges, possible resonances, broadband noise, and one-off events before changing filters.
questions: Does the energy move with throttle or measured motor RPM?
Is a peak largely stationary, broadband, or confined to one short event?
Which mechanical and recorded-data checks should happen before filter tuning?

blocks.text: A tall peak is a location, not a confession. Spectrum helps describe how energy behaves: whether it stays nearly fixed, moves with throttle, aligns with measured motor harmonics, spreads across a broad band, or appears only during one impact or manoeuvre.

steps: Begin with Frequency to locate concentrated and broadband energy across suitable signals and axes.
Switch to Frequency vs Throttle to see whether ridges move as propulsion load changes.
Use Frequency vs RPM when eRPM was logged; confirm motor pole count before trusting mechanical-frequency alignment.
When a numeric blade count is available, compare the individually selectable blade-pass guides with the observed ridges across changing RPM.
Measure a narrower time range when the suspected behaviour was brief.
Return to Graph to see whether the energy coincides with a move, propwash recovery, impact, or motor-anomaly interval.

blocks.title: Classify the behaviour before naming the source

blocks.caption: What a spectral shape can support
rows: Throttle is not measured motor speed, and several mechanical sources can move with load.
Motor-speed linkage is stronger when eRPM and motor poles are sound.
The exact prop, motor, bearing, frame part, or mounting fault responsible.
The energy scales with motor speed at that expected blade-pass order when eRPM, motor poles, and blade count are sound.
A particular damaged prop, motor, bearing, mount, or frame part as the source.
A possible structural or component resonance deserves inspection.
That the frame alone caused it; antennas, mounts, cracked parts, props, and other structures can resonate.
Turbulence, impacts, rough mechanics, or several overlapping sources may be present.
A single filter or component as the cure.
Energy exists only in a short range
The event context matters more than a whole-flight average.
That the rest of the flight shares the same behaviour.

blocks.expression: motor frequency = logged eRPM × 3.333 ÷ motor poles
blocks.explanation: Airframe follows the current Betaflight conversion used for RPM-notch interpretation. The result is only as credible as the recorded eRPM and configured motor pole count.

The physical motor magnet-pole count configured for conversion

blocks.title: Do not diagnose from a universal red line
blocks.text: Familiar frequency regions and dB references come from particular craft classes, plots, and analysis methods. Prop size, KV, voltage, mass, stiffness, prop geometry, sample rate, windowing, and normalization all move the picture. Treat the guides as context, not pass/fail.

blocks.title: The next check may be physical
blocks.text: Inspect props, motors, bearings, fasteners, antennas, stack and camera mounting, wiring, and damaged frame parts when the evidence points toward a mechanical source. A log cannot see looseness, heat, or damage directly.

Once the behaviour is located, judge the filter result separately. That next step compares the signal path, downstream D-term and motor activity, recorded filter positions, and delay instead of asking one peak to answer every question.
